trace.claim: The paper asks whether online political hostility is associated with political engagement and its antecedents, beyond explanations based on socioeconomic marginalization, personality traits, or grievance.

Politically engaged users who express hostility also post more frequently, have more friends and followers, and thus have greater potential reach on X/Twitter, suggesting that hostile expression is linked to higher visibility and activity.

The study combines two years of survey and behavioral data from American X/Twitter users, using a word embedding approach called the Super-Unsupervised (SU) method to measure online political hostility based on linguistic proximity to political and hostile language.

The study uses a panel survey to measure political engagement indicators such as education, internal efficacy, political interest, political knowledge, and participation, and links these to behavioral data on X/Twitter activity.

Affective polarization is measured through feeling thermometer ratings of political leaders (e.g., Trump, Biden, Cruz, Sanders), and the study examines whether the association between engagement and hostility is stronger among users with higher levels of affective polarization.

The analysis employs cross-sectional and panel models, including Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Models (RI-CLPM), to assess temporal within-person associations between political engagement and hostility.
Online political hostility is positively and significantly associated with political interest, political knowledge, and online/offline participation.

Users with higher levels of affective polarization show stronger associations between political engagement and online political hostility, particularly for participatory indicators like online and offline participation.
Politically hostile users post more frequently and have more followers and friends, indicating greater activity and potential reach on X/Twitter.

The association between political engagement and online political hostility is stronger for more proximate indicators (e.g., political interest and knowledge) than for distal antecedents (e.g., education and internal efficacy).
The findings are observational and do not establish causality; time-varying confounding, reciprocal relationships, and measurement error may explain the observed associations.
The study does not establish that political engagement causes hostility, and the results should be interpreted as associational rather than causal.

The measure of affective polarization focuses on feelings toward political leaders rather than toward parties or party supporters, so the moderation results are limited to leader-directed affective polarization.

The paper situates its analysis within classical theories of political engagement and recent work on the darker sides of political engagement, extending and integrating the revisionist view that political engagement can lead to biased and antagonistic behavior.
trace.new_claim: Online political hostility is associated with several indicators of political engagement and its antecedents.

trace.claim: The paper disputes the claim that online political hostility is primarily driven by socioeconomic marginalization, status threat, or personality-based traits (such as the Dark Triad), by arguing that it is also strongly associated with political engagement and its antecedents.
trace.new_claim: The paper does not dispute that online political hostility is associated with socioeconomic marginalization, status threat, or personality-based traits, but rather examines whether online political hostility is associated with political engagement and its antecedents.
